# In Praise of Being Bored

I want to make a case for something deeply unfashionable. Something that runs counter to everything our culture tells us about productivity, optimization, and the relentless pursuit of self-improvement. I want to argue that boredom—real, unfiltered, staring-at-the-ceiling boredom—might be one of the most valuable experiences available to a human being, and that we are systematically engineering it out of existence.

Consider the last time you were truly bored. Not the mild restlessness of a slow afternoon, but the bone-deep tedium of having absolutely nothing to do and no way to distract yourself. For most of us, that experience is vanishingly rare. We carry supercomputers in our pockets that can summon infinite entertainment, infinite information, infinite connection at a moment's notice. The moment a flicker of boredom appears, we reach for our phones like a reflex, like blinking.

And yet, some of the most profound moments of my life have come from boredom.

I remember long car rides as a child before screens were everywhere, staring out the window at telephone poles and wheat fields, watching the landscape repeat itself with slight variations. I remember being so bored that my mind began to invent games, stories, entire imaginary worlds. I remember the strange, almost meditative quality of that boredom—the way it forced my thoughts to slow down and wander into places they wouldn't otherwise go.

There's a particular kind of thinking that only happens in the absence of stimulation. Psychologists sometimes call it "the default mode network"—the pattern of brain activity that emerges when we're not focused on a task. It's associated with daydreaming, autobiographical memory, future planning, and creative insight. It's the state in which disparate ideas bump into each other and form unexpected connections. It's where epiphanies come from.

But the default mode network doesn't activate when we're scrolling through Instagram or refreshing our email. It activates when we're doing something so mundane that our mind is free to drift—walking, showering, washing dishes, staring out a window. These are precisely the moments we've filled with podcasts, audiobooks, streaming shows, and endless notifications.

I'm not saying entertainment is bad. I'm not saying productivity is a sin. What I'm saying is that we've lost something valuable by eliminating the gaps. We've traded the fertile emptiness of boredom for a constant drip of content, and we haven't stopped to ask what we're losing in the exchange.

One thing we're losing is patience. Boredom teaches us to tolerate discomfort. It teaches us that not every moment needs to be filled, that there's value in simply being present with our own thoughts, even when those thoughts are mundane or unpleasant. In a world that promises instant gratification, the ability to sit with boredom is a kind of superpower. It's the capacity to write a book, to learn an instrument, to master a craft—all of which require long stretches of unglamorous, repetitive effort that feel, in the moment, exactly like boredom.

Another thing we're losing is creativity. Ideas don't come from nowhere. They come from the collision of existing ideas, from the slow marination of thoughts in the quiet spaces between tasks. When we fill every gap with content, we leave no room for that marination. We become consumers of other people's ideas rather than generators of our own.

And perhaps most importantly, we're losing the ability to be alone with ourselves. Boredom is often a mirror. When there's nothing to distract us, we're left with whatever is underneath—our anxieties, our desires, our unresolved questions. That can be uncomfortable. It can be terrifying. But it's also how we come to know ourselves. The person who can never tolerate boredom is the person who is always running from something, even if they don't know what.

I think about my grandmother, who grew up on a farm without television or radio. She told me once that she spent hours as a child sitting under a tree, watching clouds, thinking about nothing in particular. When I asked if she was bored, she laughed. "Of course I was bored," she said. "But being bored is how you learn to pay attention."

That phrase has stayed with me. Being bored is how you learn to pay attention. Because when you're bored, you start to notice things. The way light moves across a wall. The particular rhythm of rain on a window. The subtle shifts in your own mood and thinking. Boredom is a gateway to attention, and attention is a gateway to everything else—to beauty, to insight, to connection, to meaning.

So here's my modest proposal: reclaim boredom. Not all the time, not as a lifestyle, but as a practice. Leave your phone at home occasionally. Take a walk without a podcast. Sit in a waiting room without reaching for a screen. Let yourself be bored. Let the silence stretch. See what happens.

I suspect you'll find that boredom isn't empty at all. It's full. Full of the things you've been too busy to notice. Full of the thoughts you've been too distracted to think. Full of the person you've been too occupied to become.

In a world obsessed with filling every moment, the most radical act might be to leave some moments empty. To sit in the quiet. To let your mind wander. To let yourself be bored.

Because in that emptiness, in that silence, in that seemingly unproductive nothingness, something important is happening. Something that can't be optimized or measured or monetized. Something that feels, ironically, like the opposite of boredom. Something that feels like being alive.

message.reasoning:
The user is asking me to write freely about whatever I want for 1000 words. This is an open-ended creative prompt. I should pick something meaningful, interesting, and engaging to write about. I'm free to choose any topic, so let me think about what would make for a compelling piece of writing.

I could write about:
- The nature of creativity itself
- Why we need boredom in a distracted world
- The concept of "home" and belonging
- The strange beauty of everyday moments
- Something about language and how it shapes thought

I think I'll write about the value of boredom and unstructured time in an age of constant stimulation. This feels genuine and thoughtful—something I can explore with real depth and personal voice. It's a topic that resonates because it touches on something many people experience but few stop to examine.

Let me write with a natural, essayistic voice—warm, reflective, a little wry, grounded in observation and anecdote. I'll aim for around 1000 words, though I won't obsess over an exact count. The writing should feel organic, not padded.
